When the guests were leaving the warm house on Ushers Island, Gabriel Conroy noticed his wife Gretta standing motionless in the shadow of the stairs, listening to a distant voice singing an old Irish air. <break time="0.8s" /> There was grace and mystery in her attitude, as if she were a symbol of something, and Gabriel, watching from the dark hall below, thought that, were he a painter, he would paint her in that pose. <break time="0.8s" /> Later, as they made their way through the slushy streets toward the hotel, moments of their secret life together burst like stars upon his memory, and he longed to be alone with her. <break time="0.8s" /> He felt that they had escaped from their lives and duties, from home and friends, and were running away together with wild and radiant hearts to a new adventure. <break time="0.8s" /> In the hotel room Gabriel told the porter to take away the candle, for the ghostly light from the street lamp lay in a long shaft from one window to the door. <break time="0.8s" /> While Gretta stood before a large mirror, taking off her hat and cloak, Gabriel crossed to the window and looked down into the street, hoping that his emotion might calm a little. <break time="0.8s" /> When at last he turned and called her name, she walked slowly toward him along the shaft of light, and her face looked so serious and weary that the words would not pass his lips. <break time="0.8s" /> No, it was not the moment yet, he told himself, and he waited, longing to be master of her strange mood, for some sign that she was thinking of him.

To break the silence, Gabriel mentioned, in a false voice, that Freddy Malins had paid back the money he owed him, and he added that Freddy was a decent fellow after all. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly Gretta came to him, stood on tiptoe to kiss him, and said softly that he was a very generous person, and for a moment his heart trembled with a happiness he had not expected. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet when he held her close and asked what she was thinking about, she was silent at first, and only after he pressed her again did she answer that she was thinking of that song. <break time="0.8s" /> It was The Lass of Aughrim, the very song she had heard on the stairs, and as she spoke its name she broke away from him, threw herself upon the bed, and hid her face. <break time="0.8s" /> Gabriel stood still for a moment in astonishment, and then, passing the mirror on his way to her, he caught sight of himself, a man whose face always puzzled him in a glass. <break time="0.8s" /> Standing near her, he asked why the song made her cry, and between her sobs she told him that she was thinking of a person who used to sing it long ago in Galway. <break time="0.8s" /> His name was Michael Furey, she said, a delicate boy whom she had known when she was a girl living with her grandmother, and she used to go out walking with him. <break time="0.8s" /> Gabriel, a cold irony in his voice, suggested that perhaps she wanted to go to Galway to see him, but she looked away in silence and at length answered that the boy had died at only seventeen.
